title: Body and Mind
description: Ten calm columns, interviews, profiles and reviews about health of body and mind: learning to meditate, a nutritionist's case for soup, sleep and memory, a physical therapist's patient, walking as medicine, giving blood, stress at work, a meditation app, a chess grandmaster's routine and a restful week by the sea.

lessons.title: Ten Minutes of Nothing
lessons.summary: A busy accountant learns to meditate for ten minutes every morning in a corner beside her bedroom closet.
lessons.text:
For years, I believed that meditation was for other people: calm people, flexible people, people with plenty of free time. I was none of these. I was a busy accountant with a phone that never stopped buzzing, and I was not keen on sitting still. Then my doctor, after hearing me describe my sleepless nights, suggested that I try it for ten minutes a day. "It won't fix everything," she said, "but it may teach you to pause."

What I needed, I decided, was a quiet place. Our apartment is small, so I chose a corner of the bedroom, beside the closet. I put a cushion on the floor, placed a small plant beside it and called it my meditation corner. My husband, who is more keen on football than on breathing exercises, smiled politely and closed the door.

The first week was uncomfortable. My knees hurt, my back ached and my mind would not stop. The instructions in my beginner's book were simple: sit up straight, close your eyes, notice your breath, and when a thought arrives, notice it and return to the breath. Simple, but not easy. Every few seconds I remembered an email, a bill or the open closet door. Sitting still with my own thoughts was more uncomfortable than any meeting I had ever attended.

The book explained something that helped me. When we are stressed, the body reacts to a deadline or a difficult conversation as if it were a threatening animal: the heart beats faster and the muscles get tight. A short pause, with slow breathing, tells the body that nothing threatening is happening. Not once did the book promise that the thoughts would disappear. It only promised that I would get better at noticing them.

So I made it a ritual. Every morning, before coffee, I sat on the cushion beside the closet for ten minutes. A ritual, I learned, is easier to keep than a decision, because you do not have to decide again each day. Practically speaking, it meant setting the alarm ten minutes earlier, and on some mornings that was the hardest part.

After a month, something changed, although the change was practically invisible from the outside. I still had busy thoughts, but I was quicker to notice them. Sustained attention, even for a few minutes, began to feel possible, and that sustained attention stayed with me during the day. In meetings, I caught myself taking a pause before I answered, instead of reacting at once.

I would not say that I am a calm person now. But had I waited until I had more free time, I would never have started. Ten minutes, it turns out, is enough to begin.

Questions:
Why did the writer start meditating?
The writer's doctor suggested ten minutes a day after hearing about the writer's sleepless nights.
Where is the meditation corner?
It is in a corner of the bedroom, beside the closet.
Why was the first week uncomfortable?
The writer's knees and back hurt, and the writer's mind would not stop.
How does the body react to stress, according to the book?
It reacts as if there were a threatening animal nearby: the heart beats faster and the muscles get tight.
Why is a ritual easier to keep than a decision?
A ritual is easier to keep because you do not have to decide again each day.
What changed after a month?
The writer noticed busy thoughts more quickly and began to take a pause before answering in meetings.

lessons.title: In Praise of Soup
lessons.summary: A nutritionist answers January's questions about harsh diets with a calm case for soup, fruit and fiber.
lessons.text:
Every January, my inbox fills with the same question. Readers want to know which harsh diet they should start: no bread, no fruit, or nothing but juice for a week. Rarely does my answer change. Harsh rules are usually unnecessary, and they are hard to keep. What most of us need is not a stricter plan but a warmer one. This month, I would like to make the case for soup.

A good vegetable soup does many things at once. It is full of water, which helps us feel full. It is an easy way to eat several vegetables in one bowl, and it costs little to make. A simple tomato soup, made with tomatoes, onions, garlic and a little olive oil, takes about half an hour. Tomatoes are rich in vitamin C, and cooking them with a little oil helps the body absorb some of their other useful compounds. A squeeze of lemon at the end makes the flavor brighter, so you need less salt.

There is also emerging research on the bacteria that live in our gut. Most of these bacteria are not our enemies; many of them help us digest food. The research is still emerging, and careful scientists are modest about their claims, but one point is widely accepted: the friendly bacteria like fiber, which we find in vegetables, beans, whole grains and fruit. A bowl of bean and vegetable soup feeds them well.

Now, about fruit. One widespread myth says that tropical fruit, such as the banana or the mango, is "too sweet" to be healthy. It is true that a ripe banana tastes sweet, but a banana also brings fiber, and it comes in its own convenient package. Tropical fruit is not a dessert to avoid; it is a snack to enjoy, and cutting it out is unnecessary. Another widespread myth says that a glass of hot water with lemon in the morning "cleans" the body. Lemon water is pleasant, and it is a good way to drink more water, but your liver and kidneys do the cleaning, every day, at no cost.

So here is my plan for the cold months, and it is not harsh at all. Make a big pot of soup on the weekend. Keep a bowl of bananas on the kitchen table. Add lemon instead of extra salt. Eat slowly, and with other people when you can.

As always, readers with a health condition are advised to talk to their doctor before they make big changes to what they eat. Everyone else is advised to find a large pot.

Questions:
What question do readers ask every January?
They ask which harsh diet they should start.
Why does the writer like vegetable soup?
It is full of water, it is an easy way to eat several vegetables, and it costs little to make.
Why does the writer add lemon to soup?
Lemon makes the flavor brighter, so you need less salt.
What do the friendly bacteria in our gut like?
They like fiber, which we find in vegetables, beans, whole grains and fruit.
What widespread myth about tropical fruit does the writer mention?
The myth says that tropical fruit, such as the banana, is too sweet to be healthy.
Who is advised to talk to a doctor?
Readers with a health condition are advised to talk to their doctor before big changes.

lessons.title: What Sleep Does for Memory
lessons.summary: In an interview, a sleep researcher explains how sleep stores memories, why a sleep deficit matters and how light helps.
lessons.text:
Dr. Lena Ortiz studies sleep and memory at a university hospital. We spoke with her at the end of a long day of conference proceedings, where she had presented her latest work.

You have spent the whole day at the conference proceedings. Are you tired?
Very! But that is normal. Feeling tired at the end of a long day is an indication that the body is working as it should. Feeling sleepy every morning, on the other hand, can be an indication that something is wrong.

What does sleep have to do with memory?
A great deal. During the day, we collect new information. During sleep, especially deep sleep, the brain sorts that information and stores the important parts. In our lab, we teach students a list of words in the evening. Those who sleep well remember more of the list the next morning than those who stay awake. When I show this graph at a conference, the difference between the two lines is very clear.

What happens when people do not sleep enough?
They build up what we call a sleep deficit. One short night is not a disaster. After five consecutive nights of short sleep, however, most people do worse on memory tests, even if they say they feel fine. And a sleep deficit is not easy to repay. Sleeping late on one weekend morning helps, but it does not fully erase a week of short nights.

Many people attribute their poor memory to age. Are they right?
Sometimes, partly. But before I attribute anything to age, I ask people how they are sleeping. Had they slept well for the last month, many of them would be less worried about their memory now.

What about a nap?
A short nap of about 20 minutes, in the early afternoon, can help you feel more awake. A long nap late in the day, however, can make it harder to fall asleep at night.

Why do infants sleep so much?
Newborn infants sleep for most of the day, often 14 hours or more. Their brains are learning an enormous amount, and sleep is a big part of how that learning is stored. The significance of this is easy to miss. For an infant, sleep is not lost time; it is working time. That, to me, is the real significance of sleep at every age.

Is there an easy way to sleep better?
What matters most is light. In one well-known study, people who spent a week camping in a tent, with sunlight by day and no electric light at night, began to fall asleep and wake up earlier. Not everyone can live in a tent, of course! But morning light and darker evenings help most people.

Questions:
Where did the interviewer speak with Dr. Ortiz?
They spoke at the end of a long day of conference proceedings.
What does the brain do with new information during sleep?
It sorts the information and stores the important parts.
What does the graph show?
The graph shows that students who sleep well remember more words than students who stay awake.
How does a sleep deficit build up?
It builds up when people do not sleep enough, for example after five consecutive nights of short sleep.
When is a nap helpful?
A short nap of about 20 minutes in the early afternoon can help you feel more awake.
What happened to the people who spent a week in a tent?
They began to fall asleep and wake up earlier.

lessons.title: Back on Two Wheels
lessons.summary: A profile of a motorcycle rider who recovers from an accident with the help of a young physical therapist.
lessons.text:
Tom Becker has loved motorcycles since he was a teenager. For twenty years, he has ridden the same vintage motorcycle, a red machine built in 1972, which he keeps in perfect condition. Last spring, on a wet road, a car turned in front of him, and Tom fell.

His helmet did its job. The doctors told him later that it had almost certainly protected his skull from serious damage. Still, the list of injuries was long. The doctors diagnosed a broken wrist, a broken thumb and a partially torn ligament in his left knee. A partially torn ligament, they explained, can often heal without surgery, but only with months of careful exercise.

That is how Tom met Priya Shah, a physical therapist who had finished her qualification only a year before. "I was practically a rookie," she says, laughing. "Tom was one of my first long-term patients." Tom remembers it differently. "She may have been a rookie, but she knew exactly what she was doing. Her qualification was new; her patience was not."

The first weeks were slow. Priya began with the thumb and the wrist, because Tom could not hold a cup of coffee. He squeezed a soft ball a hundred times a day. Then came the knee: small bends, short walks and balance on one leg. Priya was strict about one rule: no explosive movements, which meant no jumping, no running and no sudden turns until the ligament was ready. Explosive movements put a large force on the knee in a fraction of a second, and a knee that is still healing cannot handle that force.

What impressed Priya most was Tom's determination. He never missed a session, and he did his exercises at home every evening. "Determination is the one thing I cannot give a patient," she says. "I can give them a plan. They have to bring the determination."

After four months, Priya gave Tom a test: a vertical jump, straight up, landing softly on both feet. His first vertical jump was low and careful. By the end of the month, it was almost as high as before the accident.

Not until the summer did Tom sit on his vintage motorcycle again. He rode slowly, on a quiet road, with Priya's advice in his head. He now wears better gloves to protect his hands and thumbs, and he tells every rider he meets that a good helmet is the best friend a skull can have. If he had not done all those exercises, he says, he would not be riding today.

Questions:
What kind of motorcycle does Tom ride?
He rides a red vintage motorcycle that was built in 1972.
What did the doctors diagnose after the accident?
They diagnosed a broken wrist, a broken thumb and a partially torn ligament in his left knee.
Why did Priya call herself a rookie?
She had finished her qualification only a year before, and Tom was one of her first long-term patients.
Why did Priya not allow explosive movements?
They put a large force on the knee, and a knee that is still healing cannot handle that force.
What test did Priya give Tom after four months?
She gave him a vertical jump test.
What does Priya say she cannot give a patient?
She says she cannot give a patient determination.

lessons.title: Is Walking Really Medicine?
lessons.summary: An essay weighs the case for walking as medicine against its limits and asks what cities and people can do.
lessons.text:
Doctors like to say that walking is the best medicine that nobody takes. It is a pleasant idea, but is it true? Before we put on our shoes, it is worth weighing both sides.

The case for walking is strong. Regular walking strengthens the heart, helps to control weight and blood sugar, and improves mood. Health organizations generally recommend about 150 minutes of moderate activity a week, and a quick walk of half an hour on most days meets that goal. Above all, walking is accessible. It needs no gym, no special clothes and no lessons, and most people can do it at almost any age. Exercise that is accessible to everyone is more likely to be sustainable, and a sustainable habit is worth more than an ambitious plan that lasts two weeks.

There is also a social side. A walk with a friend is a conversation that happens to be exercise. Some people find that the adoption of a dog changes their week completely: a dog does not accept excuses, so its owner walks twice a day, in rain or sun. Others walk with their grandchildren to the zoo and cover several miles without noticing, because their attention is on the animals.

The case against is more modest, but it deserves to be heard. Walking alone is not enough for everyone. Muscles and bones also need strength exercise, and walking at an easy pace does little to build strength. Nor is walking equally easy everywhere. In a large metropolitan area, the nearest park may be situated far from home, the sidewalks may be crowded, and the air may be polluted. A long street with heavy traffic and garbage on the sidewalk is not an invitation to walk. And when a city announces the closure of a park for repairs, the people who lose most are those who have nowhere else to go.

What, then, should we conclude? Walking is not magic, and it is not a complete program. But it is a very good start, and the problems are mostly problems of design, not of walking itself. Cities can avoid long closures, keep parks open, remove the garbage from the streets and make the walk to the metro safe and pleasant. Many metropolitan areas have found that people walk more when a metro station is situated within a short, safe walk of their homes. Individuals, for their part, can get off the metro one stop early, walk to the zoo instead of driving, and add some strength exercise twice a week.

Rarely is the simplest medicine the most fashionable one. In this case, it may also be the most sustainable.

Questions:
Why is walking described as accessible?
It needs no gym, no special clothes and no lessons, and most people can do it at almost any age.
How can the adoption of a dog change a person's week?
The owner has to walk the dog twice a day, in rain or sun.
What is one argument against walking alone?
Walking at an easy pace does little to build the strength that muscles and bones need.
What problems can people face in a metropolitan area?
The nearest park may be far away, the sidewalks may be crowded, and the air may be polluted.
What can cities do to help people walk?
They can keep parks open, remove the garbage from the streets and make the walk to the metro safe.
What simple step can individuals take?
They can get off the metro one stop early.

lessons.title: Why I Give Blood
lessons.summary: A regular blood donor describes her doubts at the start, the simple visit and why every donation matters.
lessons.text:
I gave blood for the first time when I was 18, mostly because my older sister dared me to. Twenty years later, I have done it more than 40 times. I am not brave, and I am not a nurse. I am simply a donor, one of many ordinary people who give an hour of their time a few times a year.

I will admit that I had reservations at the beginning. I am not fond of needles, and I was worried that I might faint. My sister listened to my reservations and then said, "The needle takes a few seconds. The person who receives your blood may need it to stay alive." I could not think of a good answer to that.

The visit itself is simple. When you arrive, you show your identification, such as a driver's license or another card with your photo. The staff check your identification, ask you a list of health questions and take your pulse, your temperature and a drop of blood from your finger. If your pulse is too fast or your iron is too low, they will ask you to come back another time. Donors must comply with these rules, and I have always been glad that they exist. They protect the donor and the recipient alike.

Then you lie down, and the donation itself takes about ten minutes. Afterward, the staff give you a drink and a snack and ask you to rest for a while. Most people feel fine. If you do not feel well, you tell the nurse, and she helps you. You must also wait several weeks before you can give blood again, a rule that every donor has to comply with.

What I did not understand at 18 was where the blood goes. A single donation can be separated into parts, such as red cells and plasma, and these parts can help more than one recipient: a patient in surgery, a person with a serious illness, or someone who was hurt in an accident. You never meet your recipient, and the recipient never meets you.

Sadly, blood centers often report that they do not have enough donors, especially in summer and during the holidays. Blood cannot be made in a factory, and it does not keep forever.

Last month, a young nurse paid me a compliment. She said that I had "excellent veins." It is a strange compliment, but I was proud of it all day. I told her that if more of my friends knew how easy it is, they would sign up tomorrow. Sadly, most of them still say they are too busy. I am working on them.

Questions:
Why did the writer give blood for the first time?
Mostly because an older sister dared the writer to do it.
What reservations did the writer have at the beginning?
The writer was not fond of needles and was worried about fainting.
What do you show when you arrive?
You show your identification, such as a driver's license or another card with your photo.
Why must donors comply with the rules?
The rules protect the donor and the recipient alike.
How can one donation help more than one recipient?
It can be separated into parts, such as red cells and plasma.
What compliment did the nurse pay the writer?
She said that the writer had excellent veins.

lessons.title: Not Everything Is Urgent
lessons.summary: A support team's manager finds that her team's stress has a structural cause, and the team builds a simple system to fix it.
lessons.text:
Last year, the eight members of the support team at a small software company were tired, and everyone could see it. The team had moved to a hybrid schedule two years earlier, with three days at home and two in the office. In theory, the hybrid model gave people flexibility. In practice, it gave them a laptop that was always open. Emails arrived late at night, chat messages arrived during lunch, and nobody felt able to step away from the keyboard.

The manager, Helen Cho, noticed the first indicator in the numbers. Attendance at the weekly team meeting had dropped, and sick days had nearly doubled. A second indicator was quieter: people had stopped joking in the team chat. "When a cheerful team goes silent," Helen says, "something is wrong."

What Helen did first was ask. She met each person alone and asked one question: what makes your week harder than it needs to be? She was surprised by how similar the answers were. Too many tasks were deemed urgent. Almost every request from another department was marked "high priority," and the team had no way to decide which ones really were.

Helen concluded that the problem was structural, not personal. Telling tired people to "manage their stress" would not fix a structural problem. So, together, the team sat down to construct a simple system. Each morning, one person read all the new requests and sorted them into three groups: today, this week and later. Only requests from customers who could not work at all were deemed urgent. Helen also learned to delegate. Instead of approving every small decision herself, she began to delegate them to experienced team members, which saved her hours each week and made people feel trusted.

The team agreed on a few more rules. Nobody was expected to answer messages after six in the evening. A short reminder appeared on every screen at noon, suggesting a break away from the keyboard. Not only did people begin eating lunch away from their desks again, but some of them also started taking short walks together. Next, they set about constructing a shared calendar that showed who was in the office on which days, so that the hybrid week felt like one team rather than two.

Six months later, attendance at the weekly meeting was back to normal, and sick days had fallen. The most important indicator, however, was the team chat, which was full of jokes again. Helen keeps one reminder on her own desk, written on a card: "Not everything is urgent."

Questions:
What kind of schedule did the team have?
They had a hybrid schedule, with three days at home and two in the office.
What was the first indicator that something was wrong?
Attendance at the weekly meeting had dropped, and sick days had nearly doubled.
Why did Helen think the problem was structural?
Too many tasks were deemed urgent, and the team had no way to decide which ones really were.
What system did the team construct?
Each morning, one person sorted the new requests into three groups: today, this week and later.
How did learning to delegate help Helen?
It saved her hours each week and made team members feel trusted.
What does the reminder on Helen's desk say?
It says, "Not everything is urgent."

lessons.title: Review: Quiet Hour
lessons.summary: A reviewer tests a meditation and sleep app for a month and weighs its beautiful lessons against its price and its unclear data policy.
lessons.text:
Quiet Hour, a meditation and sleep app, promises to help you "rest your mind anytime, anywhere." After using it every day for a month, I can say that it mostly keeps that promise, although I have a few reservations.

What you notice first is the artwork. Each lesson opens with a calm painting: a lake at dawn, a forest in fog, a single boat on still water. The artwork depicts quiet places rather than people, which leaves room for your own thoughts. The sleep section depicts the night sky, with stars that move slowly as the voice speaks. It is, quite simply, beautiful.

The lessons themselves are good. A beginner's course of ten short sessions teaches the basics of breathing and attention, and there are sleep stories, short pauses for the working day and longer sessions for the weekend. Because the sessions are on your phone, you can use them anytime: on the bus, in a waiting room or in bed at the end of a long day.

The price is less calm. The free version offers only three sessions. To use everything, you must subscribe, at 10 bucks a month or 60 bucks a year. If you subscribe for a year, the price is fair compared with other apps, but the app asks you to subscribe practically every time you open it, and that is not relaxing.

There is also the question of ethics. In recent years, there have been allegations that some health apps share information about their users with advertisers. I found no evidence that Quiet Hour does this, and I want to be clear that no such allegation has been made against it. Still, the company does not clearly disclose what data it collects, and its privacy policy is long and difficult to follow. An app about mental health should disclose these things in plain language, on one page. Good ethics, in this area, means not making users search for the answers.

Finally, there is a small contradiction. Many of us download a meditation app because we feel like phone addicts. Yet this app sends daily reminders and counts your "streak" of consecutive days, which can turn even rest into a game. I hope I am not a phone addict, but I turned the reminders off after a week, and only then did I really begin to enjoy the app.

My conclusion: beautiful artwork and thoughtful lessons, worth 10 bucks a month if you use the app often. The company should disclose more and push less.

Questions:
What does the artwork in the app depict?
It depicts quiet places, such as a lake at dawn or a forest in fog, rather than people.
When can you use the sessions?
You can use them anytime: on the bus, in a waiting room or in bed.
How much does it cost to subscribe?
It costs 10 bucks a month or 60 bucks a year.
Why does the writer raise the question of ethics?
There have been allegations that some health apps share user information, and Quiet Hour does not clearly disclose what data it collects.
Why did the writer turn the reminders off?
The reminders and the streak of consecutive days can turn even rest into a game.
What should the company do, according to the writer?
It should disclose more and push less.

lessons.title: The Grandmaster Who Goes to Bed Early
lessons.summary: A profile of a shy chess grandmaster whose results improved when she began to sleep, walk and eat well.
lessons.text:
Sara Lund became a chess grandmaster at the age of 24, and she has played in tournaments on every continent except Antarctica. Ask her about the secret of her success, however, and she will not talk about clever moves. She will talk about sleep, walking and breakfast.

As a child, Sara was painfully shy. She was the youngest of four siblings, and at the dinner table her older siblings did most of the talking. At school, a bully in her class made fun of her quiet voice, and for a while she dreaded the playground. Then a teacher started a chess club. At the chess board, Sara found that she did not need to speak. "The board was the one place where nobody could bully me," she says. "If someone was rude, I answered with my moves."

Her pursuit of the grandmaster title took nearly ten years. It was a pursuit, she says, that taught her more about the body than about chess. In her teens, she studied late into the night and often played tired. Her results were uneven: brilliant one day, careless the next. If she had kept studying until midnight, she says, she might not be a grandmaster today.

The leap forward came when a coach looked at her schedule and asked how many hours she slept. "Not enough" was the honest answer. What changed her game was not a new strategy but a new routine. She began to sleep eight hours, even during tournaments. She took a long walk every morning, whatever the weather, and she ate a proper breakfast before each game. Within a year, her rating made a leap that surprised everyone, including her. Never since then, she says, has she regretted going to bed early.

A long game of chess can last five or six hours. "People think we just sit there," Sara says. "But by the end, your heart is beating fast and your mind is exhausted. If you are tired, you make mistakes that you would never make at home."

Today, Sara is still a little shy in interviews, but she speaks easily about her family. Her three siblings now live on three different continents, and each of them follows her games online from their respective homes. During big tournaments, they send messages from their respective time zones, some late at night and some early in the morning. Sara reads them after the game, never before. Before a game, she says, all she needs is a good night's sleep.

Questions:
Where has Sara played chess?
She has played in tournaments on every continent except Antarctica.
Why did Sara like the chess club as a child?
At the chess board she did not need to speak, and nobody could bully her.
How long did her pursuit of the grandmaster title take?
It took nearly ten years.
What caused the leap forward in her results?
A coach asked how many hours she slept, and she began to sleep eight hours, walk every morning and eat a proper breakfast.
Why is a long game of chess tiring?
By the end, your heart is beating fast and your mind is exhausted.
How do her siblings follow her games?
They follow her games online from their respective homes on three different continents.

lessons.title: A Week by the Sea
lessons.summary: After a hard year, the writer rents a small cottage in a coastal village and learns to rest.
lessons.text:
Last October, after a year of long days and short nights, I did something I had never done before: I took a week off and went somewhere with nothing to do. I found a small rental cottage in a coastal village, three hours from the city. The rental had one bedroom, a tiny kitchen and a view of the sea. It had no television, and the internet was so slow that it was practically useless. I had not chosen it for that reason, but I soon came to be grateful for it.

On the first day, I did not know what to do with myself. My mind was still at work. I kept reaching for my phone, as though an important message might arrive at any moment. The list of tasks in my head felt endless. So I went for a walk along the coastal path, and I kept walking until noon.

By the third day, a pattern had formed. I woke without an alarm, usually at about seven, and walked on the beach before breakfast. In the late morning, I read on the small porch of the rental. At noon, I ate bread, cheese and tomatoes, and in the afternoon I swam. The water was cold, but after a few minutes I could lie on my back, floating, with my ears under the water and the sky above me. Floating there, I could hear nothing but my own breath. Rarely had I felt so calm.

On the fourth night, a storm came in from the sea. I watched the lightning over the water and counted the seconds until the thunder. At first the thunder was distant, a low sound far out at sea, and then it came closer until the windows shook. I am usually nervous during storms, but this time I simply listened. When the thunder became distant again, I went to bed and slept for nine hours, longer than I had slept in months.

By the end of the week, the city felt distant, too, in a good way. The endless list in my head had become a short one, and it no longer felt urgent. I had not solved any problems; I had simply rested.

I am back at work now, and the emails are as endless as before. But I have kept two habits from that week: a walk before breakfast, and lunch at noon away from my desk. If I had not taken that week, I would probably still believe that rest is a waste of time.

Questions:
Where did the writer stay during the week?
The writer stayed in a small rental cottage in a coastal village, three hours from the city.
What did the writer do on the first day?
The writer walked along the coastal path until noon.
What did the writer do in the afternoons?
The writer swam and lay floating on the water.
What happened on the fourth night?
A storm came in from the sea. The thunder was distant at first, and then it came closer.
How did the writer sleep after the storm?
The writer slept for nine hours, longer than the writer had slept in months.
What two habits did the writer keep?
The writer kept a walk before breakfast and lunch at noon away from the desk.
